clue.text: Wedding party so nearly having start delayed

indicators.note: a start that is held back arrives later than it should, so the letter at the front has to wait until the very end

parts.note: 'so' in the sense of consequently - do this, so that follows - is THEN
nigh is the old word for nearly, as in the end is nigh

explanation.walkthrough: Write the two words out and the opening T is simply sent to the back of the queue. Nothing in the wedding surface suggests a letter is running late.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen night is the bride's own celebration before the wedding, so the definition names one particular party rather than the reception.

clue.text: Notable experience swimming so deep around island

indicators.note: letters set swimming are adrift and no longer holding the line they were given
one thing placed around another encircles it, so the island finishes up enclosed rather than tacked on the end

parts.note: the two words hand over six letters to be swum about
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.walkthrough: 'Notable' is doing quiet work: not every experience qualifies, only one that stands out far enough to be told afterwards as a story.
explanation.definitionFit: An episode is a single self-contained happening in a life or a series, so it names an experience marked off from everything around it.

clue.text: Pig's head turning 180 degrees unlike before

indicators.note: the head is the first letter, read as a compass point; spinning south round by half a circle points it north

parts.note: a sow is a female pig

explanation.surface: A pig spins its head right round, which it never could in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter of SOW is S, south on a compass; 'turning 180 degrees' points it the opposite way, to N for north. 'unlike before' describes the present moment, as against then.
explanation.definitionFit: Now refers to the present time, which is set against what was the case earlier.

clue.text: Four brave nurses go out for a good time

definitions.text: go out for a good time

indicators.note: a nurse holds a patient in her care, so the word asks one piece to close protectively around another

parts.note: a gallant soldier is a brave one
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts four brave nurses on a night out; the moment you read 'nurses' as an instruction the sentence stops being about hospital staff at all.
explanation.definitionFit: To gallivant is to roam about in search of pleasure, which is going out for a good time with a faint note of disapproval attached.

clue.text: Did 25 fully pay attention to getting shirt on?

indicators.note: in a clue running down the grid, one thing worn on another sits above it, so the shirt goes on top

parts.note: a tee is the shirt you pull on over your head
to heed something is to give it your whole attention

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cross-reference: 25 down is LOL, so what is wanted is the past tense of a giggle, spelt the way comics write it.
explanation.definitionFit: LOL is what people type when something has made them laugh, and to have tee-heed is to have laughed in exactly that small written way.

clue.text: Turn odd bits of bomber jacket green

indicators.note: counting through a word, the bits in the odd positions are the first, the third and the fifth letters
a jacket goes round whatever is inside it, so as a verb the word tells one piece to wrap the other

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of bomber
eco is the everyday shorthand for green in the environmental sense

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bomber jacket' is one garment on the surface and two separate instructions underneath, and green here is not a colour but a cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Turn sour, turn nasty, turn green: in this sense 'turn' is the linking verb for changing into something, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: No-frills airline defective but let's go with it

parts.note: BA is British Airways, the crossword's default airline

parts.words: defective but let's go with it
parts.note: sic is what an editor writes beside a mistake to say it is being printed exactly as it stood

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sic' is worth banking: Latin for thus, and it always means the error you have just read was in the original and has been left alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-frills service hands you the plain thing and charges for every extra, so the adjective describes what is left once the trimmings go.

clue.text: Addicts who frequent bars never weary?

definitions.meaning: the surface sends you to the pub, where the addicts propping up the bar are drinkers - and the word for those is the one this coinage is modelled on
the bars the setter means are the ones that come wrapped, and the sugar in them is why this particular habit never flags

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to take apart here, only a pun on 'bars': move from the saloon to the confectionery aisle and the addicts change with it.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the definition, naming the habit by what is consumed, and the question mark owns up to the word being a jokey coinage built on alcoholics.

clue.text: Original guy bored by literature mounted musical

indicators.note: to bore is to drill a hole into something, so the drilled word opens up and the other piece drops inside
this clue runs down the page, so anything mounted is climbing it and reads from the bottom square upwards

parts.note: the first man in Genesis is the original guy
lit is the standard short form of literature, as in Eng Lit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mounted' does double duty on the surface, where a show is mounted rather than climbed - and Roald Dahl's schoolgirl has been a West End musical since 2011.
explanation.definitionFit: Tim Minchin's stage version of the Dahl story is what 'musical' points at, defining the name by the show it has become.

clue.text: 19C novelist amends chapter in Curious case of Oliver Twist

indicators.note: the altered pieces go into the middle of the rearranged letters
curious means odd, so these letters come out in a strange order
the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters

parts.note: the outside letters of Oliver are O and R
to amend something is to alter it, so amends means alters

explanation.surface: A Victorian-era author revises a chapter in an odd retelling of Dickens's orphan tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curious' rearranges OR (the case of Oliver) plus TWIST into SIRWOTT; ALTERS plus C (chapter) goes 'in' it after SIRW.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Scott, author of Ivanhoe and Waverley, was a leading Scottish writer of novels in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Short cone and tall cone share an end

parts.note: cone with its tail clipped
the tall cone standing on a church tower is its spire

explanation.walkthrough: Two cones, two different jobs: the first is a word to trim, the second a picture to name. And 'end' in the definition means aim, not tail.
explanation.definitionFit: People who conspire are pursuing one aim together in secret, so 'end' is used in its purpose sense - the end they have in view.

clue.text: One put off from playing gig after this?

definitions.text: One put off from playing gig after this?

indicators.note: letters that are playing are at play and move around, so the remaining pool is rearranged
the one letter is put off, that is sent away, from the pool before the rest is used

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A musician scared off performing a concert because of this nervous condition.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of GIG AFTER THIS, put off one I ('One'), and 'playing' rearranges the rest. Read as a whole, the clue also describes the answer: nerves that stop a performer going on.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage fright is the nervous dread before performing, which can make a musician pull out of a show.

clue.text: Company outing abandoned by Jack with indifference

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation tacked onto a firm's name

indicators.note: when someone abandons a party the party carries on without them, so the letter named simply walks out of the word

parts.note: a works outing at someone else's expense is a jolly
J is the jack in a pack of cards, and it is the letter that deserts

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' as a noun for a free day out is a very British sense, and the card-school jack is what leaves it. The surface reads like office gossip throughout.
explanation.definitionFit: To take news coolly is to take it without warmth or concern, which is the same as meeting it with indifference.

clue.text: Bumper possibly clipped by old lady

indicators.note: a clip fastens something inside itself, so the piece named is held within the other and not laid beside it

parts.note: ma is the old lady of the family
eg introduces an example, which is the job 'possibly' is doing

explanation.walkthrough: Bumper as an adjective - a bumper crop, a bumper issue - is the sense wanted, and the car the surface parks in front of you is there to keep you off it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bumper harvest is an unusually large one, and mega is the slang word for that same outsized scale.

clue.text: Bill wandering into Aldi further

parts.note: a bill pasted on a wall is an ad

indicators.note: a wanderer keeps to no fixed route, so letters sent wandering settle somewhere other than where they set off

parts.note: the eight letters that get shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' is the trap: it looks like a person, or the tab at the end of a meal, and it is the poster sense that pays. The supermarket keeps the surface shopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Further and additional both mean added on top of what is already there, as in a further charge or an additional charge.

clue.text: Bum drained extremely hot brew in NY's skid row

indicators.note: bum as an adjective means bad or faulty, so these letters come out wrong and rearranged
drained means emptied out, so the word keeps only its outer letters

parts.note: with its middle gone, extremely leaves only E and Y

explanation.surface: A tramp drinks the last of a scalding cup of tea on a run-down New York street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drained' empties EXTREMELY to EY; 'Bum' rearranges EY plus HOT and BREW. 'Bum' looks like the tramp of the surface but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bowery is a Manhattan street long known for flophouses and down-and-outs, the archetypal skid row.

clue.text: Enjoy security? Commission bespoke tech

parts.note: commissioning a bespoke item means getting it produced exactly to your specification; that meaning opens up into two words bracketing the tech's abbreviation between them
IT, information technology, is what an office calls its tech

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is the answer's own three words in their own order, which is the joke: one reading is a phrase about comfort, the other a plain instruction to a tailor.
explanation.definitionFit: To have it made is to be set up for life with nothing left to worry about, so the security is the idiomatic kind rather than a locked door.

clue.text: Nearly everyone puttin' on show at Christmas

parts.note: everyone is ALL, and nearly all of ALL is AL
putting on is adding, and the dropped g in puttin' says to drop the g here too

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is the whole instruction: the clue writes 'puttin'' with its g missing so that 'adding' has to lose one as well. Panto season does the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the handful of stories British theatres put on as a pantomime every December, so the definition names it by its season.

clue.text: Copper section in Dell rival's charger

indicators.note: 'in' puts what comes before it inside what comes after, so the short pieces are planted within the longer word

parts.note: Acer is the rival computer maker, and it splits to take the insertion
Cu is copper's symbol on the periodic table
s. is the abbreviation for section in a statute

explanation.walkthrough: Two traps in one line: the copper is the metal rather than the policeman, and the charger is a person bringing a charge rather than the thing a laptop plugs into.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge someone is to accuse them formally, so the one laying the charge is the accuser - a courtroom sense, not an electrical one.

clue.text: Jesus lives forever

parts.note: he lives, he is - the verb in its plainest form
ay is the old word for ever, kept alive in the phrase 'for ay'

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are exclamations rather than statements, which is the seam: a startled 'Jesus!' and a very English 'I say!' do the same job in a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouted at a surprise the name is not a prayer but an exclamation, and the answer is the mild drawing-room version of that same reaction.

clue.text: Spaniard's so long collecting silver pieces

indicators.note: to collect a thing is to gather it in, so the word doing the collecting closes around what it takes

parts.note: adios is how a Spanish speaker says goodbye
Ag is silver's chemical symbol, from the Latin argentum

explanation.walkthrough: 'So long' is a farewell, not a length of time. The definition means music: a slow movement takes its name from the tempo written at the top of the score.
explanation.definitionFit: Each one is a slow movement of a larger work, so a plural of them is a plural of musical pieces - the tempo marking has become the name.

clue.text: Grand, opulent, almost plush?

parts.note: fab, short for fabulous, means grand or splendid

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the opulent word loses its last letter

parts.note: rich means opulent, wealthy

explanation.surface: A sumptuous description of something nearly luxurious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims RICH to RIC, after FAB. The question mark marks 'plush' as an example of the answer: plush is a material.
explanation.definitionFit: Plush is a soft cloth with a long pile, so it is one kind of woven material.

clue.text: Eager to help both sides in Congo

indicators.note: the and word sits in between the two side letters
the sides of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the two outer letters of Congo
both A and B is A and B, so both gives and

explanation.surface: A volunteer keen to assist on both banks of the Congo river.
explanation.walkthrough: The two sides of CONGO are C and O; 'both' gives AND, sitting 'in' between them, so the answer reads as 'C and O'.
explanation.definitionFit: A can-do attitude is a willing, positive keenness to get things done, an eagerness to help.

clue.text: Snappy save that stops high shot?

parts.note: a snappy reply is a cross one, given with a bite
save in the sense of except - all save one, all bar one

explanation.walkthrough: Football runs right through the surface, and 'save' is the word doing the misleading: it is the preposition meaning except, not the goalkeeper's.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the beam across the top of the goal, so a shot flying too high for the keeper can still be kept out by hitting it.

clue.text: Refuse to move bowl containing dead fish from outside

indicators.note: a container holds its contents inside, so the word named opens up and the other piece sits within it

parts.note: a bowl on the table is a dish
someone who is gone is dead
eels are the fish, in the plural
you come in from outside, so the direction being named is in

explanation.walkthrough: None of the pieces line up with the words of the answer: the bowl is split in half and the phrase's own gaps fall in the middle of the chunks.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig one's heels in is to plant yourself and refuse to be shifted, an idiom borrowed from a horse braced against the reins.

clue.text: See face of lunatic that slays me

parts.note: lo! is the old imperative for look or see, as in lo and behold

indicators.note: the face of a word is the letter it presents first, the one at the very front

parts.note: the letter at the front of lunatic

explanation.walkthrough: Texting shorthand in a cryptic is newer than it looks, and the definition is the same joke a century older: being killed by something funny.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a thing slays you means it made you laugh helplessly, which is what the three texted letters report.

clue.text: Punches landed excessively on your ear

indicators.note: what falls on your ear is what you hear, so the words are taken by sound

parts.note: landed means won, as in landing a prize, and excessively means too: said together, won too

explanation.surface: A boxer's blows that connected far too often, as heard on the sound of the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'landed' gives WON and 'excessively' gives TOO; said aloud, 'won too' sounds like the answer. 'on your ear' marks the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: In boxing a one-two is a quick pair of blows, a jab followed by a cross.

clue.text: Suspect solitary enemy of Republican

indicators.note: something suspect is not what it should be, and letters that are not what they should be have been moved about

parts.note: the eight letters of solitary are the whole of the raw material

explanation.walkthrough: The capital R makes it look like American politics; the quarrel being named is the much older one between crowns and republics.
explanation.definitionFit: One side wants a monarch on the throne and the other wants none, so the two words stand as natural opponents.
